directAnswer: St. Clement I was the fourth bishop of Rome and the author, by ancient testimony, of the Letter to the Corinthians known as First Clement, one of the oldest Christian writings outside the New Testament. He is counted among the Apostolic Fathers, and Tertullian said he was ordained by St. Peter. A later legend holds that he was exiled to the Crimea and martyred by being thrown into the sea with an anchor.

sections.h2: A Bishop Who Knew the Apostles
paras: Irenaeus of Lyons places Clement third after Peter and says he had seen the blessed apostles and conversed with them, so that their preaching still echoed in his ears. Tertullian, writing around 200, reports that the Roman Church claimed Clement had been ordained by Peter himself. Origen and Eusebius suggested that he was the Clement Paul names as a fellow worker in Philippians 4:3, though that identification is uncertain.

Nothing reliable survives about his family or early life. A body of later fiction, the Clementine Recognitions and Homilies, makes him a noble Roman who traveled with Peter, but scholars regard these works as third- and fourth-century romances, not history.

sections.h2: First Clement and the Crisis at Corinth
paras: Clement’s lasting importance comes from a letter the Church of Rome sent to the Church of Corinth, usually dated to the mid-90s. Some younger members at Corinth had removed their presbyters from office, and the Roman Church wrote at length to urge repentance, humility, and the restoration of the rightful leaders. The letter does not name its author, but Dionysius of Corinth, around 170, said his church still read aloud the letter written through Clement, and later writers agree.

The letter argues that the apostles appointed bishops and deacons and made provision for others to succeed them, so legitimately appointed ministers should not be thrown out. This makes First Clement an early witness to apostolic succession and to Rome’s concern for another church’s peace, though historians debate how far it reflects papal authority in the later sense. It also contains one of the earliest references to the martyrdom of Peter and Paul.

sections.h2: The Anchor, the Crimea, and San Clemente
paras: Clement is named among the martyrs in the Roman Canon, but the details of his death come from a legendary Acts written in the fourth century or later. According to that account, Emperor Trajan exiled him to work in the mines near Chersonesus in the Crimea, where his preaching won converts, and he was then executed by being thrown into the Black Sea tied to an anchor. The anchor became his emblem in Christian art. Early historians such as Eusebius do not mention a martyrdom.

In the ninth century, Sts. Cyril and Methodius brought relics they believed to be Clement’s from the Crimea to Rome, where they were placed in the Basilica of San Clemente. That church, built over a fourth-century basilica and earlier Roman structures, remains a well-known pilgrimage site. Clement’s feast is November 23 in the Western Church.

keyFacts: Fourth bishop of Rome and one of the Apostolic Fathers
Author, by ancient testimony, of First Clement to the Church of Corinth (c. 96)
Tertullian reports he was ordained by St. Peter
Martyrdom by anchor in the Crimea comes from later legend
Relics brought to Rome by Sts. Cyril and Methodius; venerated at San Clemente
Named in the Roman Canon; feast day November 23

faqs.question: What is the First Letter of Clement about?
faqs.answer: It is a letter from the Church of Rome to the Church of Corinth, where some members had deposed their presbyters. It calls for repentance and peace and argues that ministers appointed in succession from the apostles should not be removed. Ancient writers attribute it to Clement, though the letter itself does not name him.

faqs.question: Why is St. Clement shown with an anchor?
faqs.answer: A later legend says he was exiled to the Crimea under Trajan and executed by being thrown into the sea tied to an anchor. The story is not found in the earliest sources, but the anchor became his traditional symbol.

faqs.question: Is Pope Clement I the Clement mentioned by St. Paul?
faqs.answer: Possibly. Origen and Eusebius identified him with the Clement whom Paul calls a co-worker in Philippians 4:3, but the name was common, and modern historians consider the link uncertain.
